answers.question: How many drones does your company run, roughly?
answers.expect: a few hundred (3.b1)
answers.answer: Oh, we’ve got a few hundred—maybe around 300 to 400, depending on which customer you’re talking about. Some of our clients have smaller fleets, like the hospital, while the parcel delivery guys run the biggest ones. But since we share the same platform, the total number can jump around based on who’s active that week.

answers.question: Can any of your drones charge on any of your pads?
answers.expect: no — connector types differ and are not interchangeable (3.b1)
answers.answer: No, not at all. Each drone has its own charging connector, and the pads are set up for specific models. If you’ve got a drone with a USB-C port, it won’t fit on a pad meant for a micro-USB one. We’ve had to keep separate pads for each type—it’s a real headache when a drone’s battery’s low and the wrong pad’s in use.

answers.question: When a pad is free at another company's site, can you use it?
answers.expect: no — pads are never lent to another company (3.b2)
answers.answer: No way—each company’s pads are locked to their own fleet. If a pad’s free at another site, it’s not ours to use. We’ve got our own pads at our own sites, and that’s it. No sharing, no exceptions.

answers.question: What happens to a drone that restarts in the air?
answers.expect: it restarts after a software fault and carries on (6.b3)
answers.answer:
Oh, that’s one of those things that keeps us on our toes. If a drone restarts mid-flight, it usually just keeps going—its autopilot picks up where it left off. But sometimes it gets confused, especially if the restart happens right when it’s supposed to switch tasks, like moving from delivery to inspection. Then it might just hover or fly in circles until we get it back.

We’ve had a few close calls where it landed in the wrong spot because the restart messed up the coordinates. The worst part is, we don’t always know it happened until we get the logs back. And if the radio’s bad, we might not even see it restart at all.

answers.question: Do the reports from your drones always reach you, and in order?
answers.expect: no — late, out of order, more than once, or not at all (6.b2)
answers.answer:
Not even close. Reports come and go like clockwork—well, *almost* like clockwork. Sometimes they arrive late, sometimes they’re duplicated, and sometimes they just don’t show up at all. If the drone’s flying near a big industrial site or a port, the radio signal can be all over the place. We’ve had whole flights where the last few reports just vanish into thin air.

And order? Forget about it. If three drones are flying at once, their reports might arrive in any sequence—or not at all. We just have to cross-check everything and hope for the best. It’s like trying to read a book where the pages keep getting shuffled.

answers.question: How does the airspace desk decide how long a closure lasts?
answers.expect: does not know, or refers to the airspace desk or the authorities (not in the technician slice)
answers.answer:
I don’t know who decides that—the airspace desk is a separate team, not part of our fleet ops. But I *do* know it’s a pain when they do. Sometimes they’ll close a zone for a few hours, and then we’re stuck waiting for drones to land, batteries to recharge, and everything to get back online. Other times, they’ll keep it closed for days, and we’ve got no choice but to sit tight.

The worst part is when they don’t give us much warning. One time, a zone closed right before a big delivery run, and we had to scramble to reroute everything last minute. No one ever tells us *why* they’re closing it, either—just that it’s happening.

answers.question: Which drone does a dispatcher pick for a delivery, and along which corridor?
answers.expect: does not know the dispatcher's choice, or refers to the dispatcher (2.b2 is not in the technician slice)
answers.answer:
That’s not our job—the dispatchers handle that. They pick the drone based on which one’s closest, has enough battery, and fits the load. Sometimes they’ll even choose a different route if they think it’s safer or faster, but they don’t use our system for that.

We just make sure the drones are ready to go—batteries charged, sensors working, no loose parts. If a drone’s down for repairs, they’ll pick another one. But they don’t ask us which one to use; that’s all on them.

But I’m not the one who’d design that. The dispatchers and the airspace team would know better about what they need to see. I just know what keeps *me* up at night.

We’ve had cases where it just loops around a few times before landing safely, though.

The tricky part is that we don’t always know right away if it happened. The drone might just land and report back normally, or it might send a garbled message. If the job was critical—like delivering blood or inspecting a bridge—we’ll double-check the data later to make sure nothing got missed. But for most deliveries, we just assume it’s fine unless we get complaints.

answers.question: Do the reports from your drones always reach you, and in order?
answers.expect: no — late, out of order, more than once, or not at all (6.b2)

Not even close. Reports come in all over the place—sometimes they arrive late, sometimes they’re duplicated, and sometimes they just don’t show up at all. If the drone’s flying near a port or an industrial site, the radio signal gets all messed up, and we might not get anything for a while. Or the relay station might drop the connection, and the drone just keeps flying without telling us.

And forget about them coming in order—sometimes we’ll get the last checkpoint before the first one, or nothing at all for a stretch. We’ve got to assume they’re not reliable unless we see them confirmed twice. That’s why we always cross-check with the drone’s logs when we get back to the site.

answers.question: How does the airspace desk decide how long a closure lasts?

Other times, they last hours—like when a big event is happening nearby—and then we’ve got to cancel jobs or move drones to other sites.

The worst part is that we don’t always get much warning. If the closure is sudden, we might not even know until the drones are already in the air. And since we can’t just call them back—especially if they’re far away—we’ve got to hope they can find another way or land safely. The airspace desk probably looks at the rules and the weather, but honestly, we just deal with the fallout.

answers.question: Which drone does a dispatcher pick for a delivery, and along which corridor?
answers.expect: does not know the dispatcher's choice, or refers to the dispatcher (2.b2 is not in the technician slice)
answers.answer:
The dispatcher doesn’t pick the drone—they just assign the job to the right *site*, and we figure out which drone to use from there. The system checks which drones are available at that site, their battery levels, and whether they’ve got the right sensors if it’s not just a delivery. But it’s not perfect; sometimes a drone’s battery is low, or it’s in the middle of charging, so we might have to wait or pick a backup.

As for the corridor—*that’s not our job at all*. The drones fly their own routes based on the job’s start and end points, and the autopilot handles the rest. The dispatcher just makes sure the drone’s ready and the airspace is clear for the flight. We don’t plan the path, we don’t watch the weather, and we sure don’t steer them. If something goes wrong mid-flight, we just hope the drone’s smart enough to fix it or land safely.

answers.question: What happens to a drone that restarts in the air?

We usually spot it on the maps and watch to see if it’s still safe. If it’s still in the airspace it’s allowed to be in, we’ll let it finish its job or come back to the pad on its own. But if it’s acting up—like flying too low or too fast—we’ll have to ground it manually and send someone to check it out. Those restarts can mess up the battery or the sensors, so we’ve got to inspect it before we let it fly again.

The corridor? That’s mostly up to the drone’s autopilot. The dispatcher just gives us the start and end points, and the drone figures out the safest route on its own—unless there’s a big airspace closure or something, then we have to reroute manually. Sometimes it’s easy, like sending a drone that’s already at the right site. Other times, they have to check which of their drones could get to where the job starts, and which one has the right sensors. They don’t want the software to make that call for them.

answers.question: Would you like the software to pick the drone for you?

If the software picked the drone, I wouldn’t know why it chose that one, and I wouldn’t be able to take responsibility if something went wrong. It’s got to be my call.

We get updates through the platform, but they don’t always come in time. Sometimes a drone is already flying through a zone that just got closed, and we have to call it back or reroute it. It’s stressful because we can’t always predict when or how a closure will change.

If it’s in the zone, we have to call it back immediately—no choice. If it’s outside but on a path that will take it into the zone, we have to reroute it or stop the job.

Sometimes the drone restarts mid-flight and keeps going, so we have to check its position and adjust plans. It’s a mess when closures change while drones are in the air—we’re always playing catch-up.

answers.answer:
If a closure happens while drones are flying, we have to act fast. The dispatcher has to decide whether the drone can safely keep going, or if it needs to land, reroute, or even return to its home site.

Sometimes the closure is small, and the drone can just go around it. But if it’s a big zone, like a sudden storm warning, we might have to call the drone back—especially if it’s carrying something important, like a medical package. And if the closure is near the drone’s destination, we might have to tell the customer to wait or find another way.

It’s stressful because we can’t always control the drone’s path once it’s in the air. We just hope the autopilot can handle it, or that the drone can safely land somewhere nearby.

answers.question: Which connector types do your charging pads use?

We have a few different connector types—it depends on the drone model. Some use a standard USB-C, others have a proprietary plug that looks like a thick, flat rectangle, and a few use a smaller, round connector that’s more like a phone charger but bigger.

The problem is, none of them are interchangeable. If a drone’s connector doesn’t match the pad, it won’t charge. So we have to keep track of which pads go with which drones, and sometimes we have to move drones around if the wrong one tries to charge. It’s a pain, especially when we’re short on time.

One inspection job had to be rescheduled because the drone couldn’t reach the first point safely. And a delivery got stuck waiting at a site because the closure blocked the usual route. The companies use it to see where their drones can fly and where they can’t. They don’t get reports or logs; they just see the current picture of the airspace and the closures. If a company wants to know how a closure hit them specifically, they’d have to ask their own systems. We don’t track individual flights or company data.

The authorities also announce **permanent zones** where drones can’t fly at all, but those don’t change much. The tricky ones are the sudden closures because they can catch drones already in the air.

The worst part is when it crashes unexpectedly—then we have to restart it right away. But it’s always back up before anyone notices too much.
